title: 第十七章 试探
content_zh:
秦伯落脚的地方，是城西一处破庙改的窝。

    说是庙，早不供神了。神像剩个泥座子，金漆剥得精光，蛛网从房梁一直挂到佛龛。庙里头横七竖八住着七八户人家，多半是进城讨生活的、逃荒来的，用破席子、烂门板隔出一小格一小格的地盘，各过各的。

    秦伯占了西墙角那一小块。一张破草席，一只旧药箱，墙上钉了几根木钉，挂着晒干的草药，散着一股子苦香。

    “将就着住。”秦伯掀开半幅破帘子，“城里寸土寸金，能有片瓦遮头，已是托了佛祖的福——虽说这佛祖自个儿都快淋成泥了。”

    江砚吃了顿饱饭。

    是秦伯用城门口剩下的几个铜钱，买的两碗热汤面，撒了点葱花。江砚捧着那粗瓷碗，吃得太急，被烫了舌头，眼泪都出来了，也舍不得停。

    逃出来这些天，这是他头一回吃上热的。

    吃完，浑身的血气像是慢慢回来了些。脱力的那种虚，淡了一点。他靠在冰凉的庙墙上，看秦伯就着窗口的天光，慢条斯理地碾药。

    秦伯没再问他来路。

    问他叫什么，他答“江砚“。秦伯“唔“了一声，说这名字好，砚是磨墨的，文气。又问他可识字，他点头。秦伯就笑，说难得，乱世里识字的孩子不多了。

    夜里，庙里渐渐安静下来。

    各家各户的隔断后头，鼾声、咳嗽声、孩子梦里的呓语，此起彼伏。秦伯也睡了，背对着江砚，呼吸绵长。

    江砚却睡不着。

    他从怀里，摸出了那柄铁片刀。

    借着佛龛前一盏将熄不熄的长明灯——也不知是哪户人家点的——他翻来覆去地看这柄刀。

    刀很丑。说是刀，不过是块巴掌长的铁片，一头被他攥得发亮，一头开了个粗糙的刃，刃口还卷着。就这么个东西，那夜在柴房里，是他抓起一截烧火炭，在土墙上没命狂涂、涂出来的。

    涂的什么，他自己都说不清。一团乱麻似的鬼画符。

    可它成真了。它割断了绳子。它让他从那必死的绝境里，逃了出来。

    代价是——他呕了血，脱力得像害了一场大病，到现在都没缓过来。

    江砚盯着这柄刀，心里翻江倒海。

    这力量，是真的。

    不是错觉，不是做梦。从沈家村那间破屋，到冰河边，到被江狗剩按在泥里那一回……那一次次“差一点“，原来都不是他疯魔。是真的有这么一桩邪门的、说出去没人信的本事，长在了他身上。

    那么——

    它到底是怎么成的？

    那夜在柴房，他是被逼到了绝路，满心都是“要活、要割断绳子“，一笔不停地狂涂。可在沈家村那么多次，他也想啊，他也急啊，怎么就没成？

    差在哪？

    江砚的心，怦怦跳起来。

    他想试。

    他得弄明白，这本事，是凭运气撞上的，还是有门道可循。要是能摸透了，能想用就用——那他往后，就再不必任人鱼肉。

    他朝秦伯那边看了一眼。老人睡得沉。

    江砚悄悄起身，挪到墙角最暗的地方，背对着所有人。

    他没有笔，也没有炭。摸了半天，从地上捡起一小截烧黑的柴头。纸更没有，他就盯上了脚边一块还算平整的青砖地面。

    写什么？

    他第一个想到的，是一只碗。

    刚才那碗热汤面，太香了。他想，要是能凭空变出一只碗，往后讨饭、喝水，都方便。多简单的东西，一只碗。

    他握住柴头，闭上眼，把那只粗瓷碗，在脑子里过了一遍。圆口，鼓肚，碗底一圈没上釉的糙脚……
content_en:
The place where Uncle Qin settled was a converted temple in the west of the city.

    It is said to be a temple, but it has long ceased to worship gods. All that's left of the statue is a clay base, the gold paint has been peeled off, and cobwebs hang from the beams to the shrine. The temple is dotted with seven or eight families, most of whom came to the city to seek a living or escape from famine. They use shabby mats and rotten door panels to separate small squares of land for each person to live in his own way.

    Uncle Qin occupied the small area in the west corner. There was a broken straw mat, an old medicine box, a few wooden nails nailed to the wall, and dried herbs hanging there, exuding a bitter fragrance.

    "We'll settle here." Uncle Qin opened half of the torn curtain, "Every inch of land in the city is valuable, and having a tile to cover your head is a blessing from the Buddha - even though the Buddha himself was almost turned into mud from the rain."

    Jiang Yan had a full meal.

    It was Uncle Qin who bought two bowls of hot soup noodles with a few coins left at the city gate, and sprinkled some chopped green onions. Jiang Yan held the coarse porcelain bowl and ate so hastily that his tongue was burned and tears came out, and he couldn't bear to stop.

    After escaping for days, this was the first time he had eaten something hot.

    After eating, the blood in my body seemed to slowly come back. The feeling of being exhausted is a little lighter. He leaned against the cold temple wall and watched Uncle Qin grinding the medicine slowly in the light of the window.

    Uncle Qin didn't ask him where he came from again.

    When asked what his name was, he replied "Jiang Yan". Uncle Qin said "no" and said that the name was good, the inkstone was polished, and it was elegant. Asked if he could read again, he nodded. Uncle Qin laughed and said it was rare. There were not many literate children in troubled times.

    At night, the temple gradually became quiet.

    Behind the partitions of each house, sounds of snoring, coughing, and children murmuring in their dreams could be heard one after another. Uncle Qin also fell asleep, with his back to Jiang Yan and his breathing long.

    Jiang Yan couldn't sleep.

    He took out the iron knife from his arms.

    With the help of an ever-burning lamp in front of the Buddhist niche—it was unknown which family lit it—he turned over the knife and looked at it.

    The knife is ugly. It was said to be a knife, but it was just a piece of iron as long as a palm. One end was shiny when he held it, and the other end had a rough blade with the edge still curled. It was just this thing. That night in the woodshed, he grabbed a piece of charcoal and scribbled it on the earthen wall.

    He couldn't tell what he was applying. A mess of ghostly drawings.

    But it came true. It cuts the rope. It allowed him to escape from the desperate situation of death.

    The price was - he vomited blood and was so exhausted that he felt like he was suffering from a serious illness, and he still hasn't recovered yet.

    Jiang Yan stared at the knife, feeling overwhelmed.

    This power is real.

    It's not an illusion, it's not a dream. From the shabby house in Shenjia Village, to the glacier, to the time when Jiang Gou Shen was pinned in the mud... those "almost" times, it turned out that he was not crazy. It is true that he has such an evil ability that no one would believe if he told it.

    Then——

    How did it come about?

    That night in the woodshed, he was forced into a corner, and his thoughts were all about "living and cutting the rope", and he kept scribbling wildly. But he had been thinking about it so many times in Shenjiacun, and he was also anxious, so why didn't it happen?

    What's the difference?

    Jiang Yan's heart started pounding.

    He wanted to try.

    He had to figure out whether he had this ability by luck or whether there was a way to do it. If he can understand it thoroughly and use it whenever he wants - then he will never have to let mermaids take advantage of him again.

    He glanced in Uncle Qin's direction. The old man slept soundly.

    Jiang Yan quietly stood up and moved to the darkest corner of the wall, facing away from everyone.

    He had no pen and no charcoal. After searching for a long time, I picked up a small piece of blackened firewood from the ground. There was no paper, so he stared at a relatively flat blue brick floor at his feet.

    What to write?

    The first thing he thought of was a bowl.

    The bowl of hot noodle soup just now was so delicious. He thought that if he could conjure a bowl out of thin air, it would be convenient for him to beg for food and drink water. Such a simple thing, a bowl.

    He held the end of the firewood, closed his eyes, and went through the rough porcelain bowl in his mind. The bowl has a round mouth, a bulging belly, and a circle of unglazed rough feet at the bottom of the bowl...
